title: Five Ways to Turn a Stimulus into a Current

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What makes a sensory neuron primary?
cards.back: It detects a stimulus and carries the signal into the nervous system itself, on its own axon.
cards.quote: A primary sensory neuron detects the stimulus and carries the signal into the nervous system itself:
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: A receptor cell that detects a stimulus and passes the signal to a separate afferent is a {{c1::secondary receptor cell}}.
cards.back: Hair cells and type II taste cells use this architecture.
cards.quote: A secondary receptor cell detects the stimulus and passes on a signal to a separate afferent,
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Why does knowing that a sensory cell is secondary not tell you whether its transduction uses an enzyme cascade?
cards.back: Primary versus secondary describes how the signal leaves the cell; direct gating versus a cascade describes what lies between stimulus and pore.
cards.quote: This is cell architecture, not transduction mechanism, so the two questions are independent.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Deflection of a hair-cell bundle pulls on {{c1::tip links}} to open transduction channels.
cards.back: Force acts on mechanically linked channel complexes without an intervening enzyme cascade.
cards.quote: Deflection of the bundle pulls on tip links and opens transduction channels in the bundle
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: What kind of channel mediates insect odorant detection, and which two receptor components form the complex?
cards.back: A ligand-gated channel formed by a tuning odorant receptor and the co-receptor Orco.
cards.quote: A tuning odorant receptor pairs with the co-receptor Orco around a central pore,
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: How does a fall in cGMP after light absorption change a rod’s membrane voltage?
cards.back: It hyperpolarizes the rod: cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels close, reducing positive charge entry.
cards.why: Light activates rhodopsin, then transducin and PDE6; the cascade lowers cGMP.
cards.quote: falling cGMP closes cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels, so less positive charge enters and the rod hyperpolarizes.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Why does an odour-driven rise in cAMP depolarize a vertebrate olfactory neuron?
cards.back: cAMP opens cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels and recruits a chloride current, producing depolarization.
cards.quote: to raise ciliary cAMP, which opens the same family of channels and recruits a chloride current, so odour depolarizes the cell.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Mouse type II taste cells release ATP through {{c1::CALHM1/3}} channels.
cards.back: Their sweet, bitter and umami detection uses GPCR cascades; ATP output uses a channel instead of vesicles.
cards.quote: releases ATP through the CALHM1/3 channel instead of vesicles.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Why can an enzyme cascade provide amplification while adding delay before a sensory current begins?
cards.back: Enzyme turnovers let one stimulus event change many molecules, but molecular encounters and reactions must occur before channels change.
cards.quote: Those turnovers let one stimulus event change thousands of molecules, and they are also a likely source of delay.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Purified rat TRPV1 and turtle hair-cell channels both lack an intervening enzyme cascade. Must they have similar activation speeds, and why?
cards.back: No. Direct gating does not set a fixed speed: about 3.5 ms was reported for purified rat TRPV1 after a heat jump versus a time constant as short as about 50 μs for turtle hair-cell channels. Preparations and protocols differ.
cards.quote: The two come from different preparations and protocols, so direct gating alone does not set a channel's speed.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: A newly studied receptor cell has force-gated channels and signals a separate afferent. Classify its architecture and transduction, then predict whether these determine its stimulus-to-movement latency.
cards.back: It is a secondary receptor cell with no intervening enzyme cascade. Those labels do not determine behavioural latency. The rules classify output architecture independently of gating, and direct gating constrains the cell’s current rather than downstream movement.
cards.quote: This is cell architecture, not transduction mechanism, so the two questions are independent.
cards.section: Two questions for any sensory cell

cards.front: Why can a hair-cell channel activation time constant and a rod’s single-photon time to peak not measure the delay caused by an enzyme cascade?
cards.back: They measure different events: the scale of a channel-current rise versus the peak of a whole-cell response. Their gap illustrates scale, not an isolated cascade delay.
cards.quote: Read the gap as a picture of scale, not as a measured cost of the cascade.
cards.section: The two designs side by side

cards.front: Why does the absence of an enzyme cascade in hair-cell transduction not mean that each stimulus moves only one ion?
cards.back: Many ions pass through each open channel, and one bundle deflection can affect many channels. Messenger multiplication and electrical current are different comparisons.
cards.quote: Both currents are then carried by many ions through each open channel, so the first row compares branching, not electrical gain.
cards.section: The two designs side by side

cards.front: What did the corrected 40-microsecond delay at 22 degrees C in the bullfrog sacculus experiment measure?
cards.back: A tissue response latency: the delay from hair-bundle stimulation to the summed transepithelial electrical response, not one channel’s opening time.
cards.quote: recorded the transepithelial microphonic, the summed electrical response across the sheet of cells.
cards.section: Forty microseconds: what a fast number measures (Corey and Hudspeth 1979)

cards.front: Why was the recorded bullfrog sacculus response delay longer than the corrected transduction delay?
cards.back: The epithelium’s electrical time constant slowed the recorded signal. Correcting that filtering reduced the inferred delay.
cards.quote: The electrical time constant of the epithelium slows such a signal, so the recorded delay is longer than the true one.
cards.section: Forty microseconds: what a fast number measures (Corey and Hudspeth 1979)

cards.front: Why does the bullfrog’s 40-microsecond tissue response constrain, rather than disprove, a messenger-mediated transduction mechanism?
cards.back: The short budget restricts messenger activation, production, diffusion and binding. Without enzyme numbers, geometry and the detectable-current threshold, it cannot exclude every messenger mechanism.
cards.quote: These numbers constrain a messenger mechanism but do not set the enzyme number or location it would need, or rule it out;
cards.section: Forty microseconds: what a fast number measures (Corey and Hudspeth 1979)

cards.front: The number of output events per input event is a {{c1::molecular gain}}, rather than a latency.
cards.back: For example, count downstream complexes per activated receptor.
cards.quote: The 2000 cGMP is a molecular gain.
cards.section: Four quantities that are often merged

cards.front: A sensory-neuron recording measures the delay from delivery of an odour pulse to the first spike. Why can this delay not be assigned entirely to channel activation?
cards.back: It includes stimulus delivery, membrane charging and spike initiation as well as transduction. It is a single-cell spike latency, not a channel activation time constant.
cards.quote: it is one cell's latency to a spike, and it includes solution exchange, membrane charging and spike initiation as well as transduction.
cards.section: Four quantities that are often merged

cards.front: A perturbation delays withdrawal from heat, but no receptor current is recorded. Does the delay establish slower heat-channel activation, and why?
cards.back: No. Behavioural latency includes conduction, spinal circuits and muscle as well as sensory transduction; the delay does not isolate channel activation.
cards.quote: These are preparation-specific numbers and must not be combined into one description.
cards.section: Four quantities that are often merged

cards.front: For illustration, combine about 2000 cGMP hydrolysed per photon in mouse rods with 13 effective transducin-PDE complexes per activated rhodopsin. What is the implied yield per complex, and is it measured?
cards.back: 2000/13 = 153.8, roughly 150 cGMP per effective complex. This is an illustrative combination, not a measured yield: the studies differed, and the complex estimate used Gcaps-null rods.
cards.quote: The two studies did not measure these together, and Yue's rods were Gcaps-null, so 150 is an illustration, not a measured yield per complex.
cards.section: Where a cascade's gain comes from, and what it costs

cards.front: Why is high molecular gain alone insufficient for a rod to signal a single photon reliably?
cards.back: Low dark noise and a reproducible elementary response are needed too; gain alone does not ensure reliable detection.
cards.quote: Gain alone does not explain it: low dark noise and a reproducible elementary response are needed too.
cards.section: Where a cascade's gain comes from, and what it costs

cards.front: An olfactory receptor becomes more spontaneously active while downstream amplification stays unchanged. What happens to receptor-origin noise, and why?
cards.back: More spontaneous events enter the cascade and are amplified. The same cascade that multiplies stimulus-driven receptor events also multiplies spontaneous receptor events.
cards.quote: A cascade that multiplies a receptor event also multiplies a spontaneous receptor event.
cards.section: Where a cascade's gain comes from, and what it costs

cards.front: Design a fair comparison of signal-to-noise ratio in a directly gated sensory cell and a cell with an enzyme cascade. Why is gain alone insufficient?
cards.back: Compare responses and noise under matched stimulus statistics, bandwidth and conditions. The governing rules are that amplification can multiply spontaneous receptor events and that the effect on signal-to-noise ratio depends on where noise enters.
cards.quote: Whether that costs signal-to-noise ratio depends on where noise enters;
cards.section: Where a cascade's gain comes from, and what it costs

cards.front: In type II taste cells from mice at least 52 days old, Calhm3 deletion abolished taste-evoked ATP release but preserved excitability. Which stage failed?
cards.back: The output stage: CALHM1/3 carries the ATP signal onward after detection, rather than serving as the stimulus-detecting receptor cascade.
cards.quote: The failure sits at the output step, after the receptor cascade has done its work.
cards.section: Detect, then send: CALHM1/3 (2018)

cards.front: For a channel starting closed in a single-exponential teaching model, activation is a(t) = {{c1::1 − exp(−t/τ)}}.
cards.back: a(t) is a fraction of maximal activation, not transmitter release.
cards.quote: a channel that starts closed reaches a fraction a(t) = 1 − exp(−t/τ) of its maximal activation.
cards.section: Detect, then send: CALHM1/3 (2018)

cards.front: A channel starts closed and follows a(t) = 1 − exp(−t/τ). During a 3 ms square pulse, what fractions of maximal activation occur for τ = 10 ms and τ = 500 ms, and what is their ratio?
cards.back: Fast: 1 − exp(−3/10) = 0.2592, or 25.9%. Slow: 1 − exp(−3/500) = 0.005982, or 0.598% (about 0.60%). Their ratio is about 43.3. These are model activation fractions, not amounts of ATP released.
cards.quote: The measured slow time constant was above 500 ms, so in this model the slow fraction would be smaller still and the ratio larger.
cards.section: Detect, then send: CALHM1/3 (2018)

cards.front: In a mouse isolated type II taste preparation, GPCR stimulation recruits PLCβ2, but IP3-dependent calcium release is blocked. What happens to calcium-driven TRPM5 activation, and why?
cards.back: It is prevented: in this pathway the released calcium activates TRPM5, so blocking the calcium rise interrupts that activation step.
cards.quote: GPCR stimulation recruits PLCβ2 and IP3-dependent calcium release, and the calcium rise activates TRPM5.
cards.section: Detect, then send: CALHM1/3 (2018)

cards.front: Which five evidence categories support identifying a protein as a sensory transducer?
cards.back: Correct place and time; loss or clear alteration of native current when it and any redundant partner are removed; permeation changes from mutation; sufficiency in an insensitive system; kinetics compatible with the native response.
cards.quote: Calling a protein the transducer asks for five kinds of evidence:
cards.section: The checklist for calling something the transducer

cards.front: Why does losing a sensory current after deleting a protein not establish that the protein forms the channel pore?
cards.back: An essential accessory protein can also be required for current. Loss establishes necessity for that current, while a pore claim needs additional evidence.
cards.why: The design problem states that removing an accessory protein could also eliminate the current.
cards.quote: Mutating it should change permeation in a way that is hard to explain indirectly,
cards.section: The checklist for calling something the transducer

cards.front: Otop1 deletion eliminated proton current in isolated mouse type III taste cells, yet knockout mice retained acid avoidance in the tested two-bottle assays. What does that establish?
cards.back: OTOP1 is necessary for that cellular current, while those behavioural assays can use other routes. Retained avoidance does not establish that the current has no role.
cards.quote: necessity for a current in a cell is not necessity for the behaviour.
cards.section: The checklist for calling something the transducer

cards.front: Purified TRPV1 supports heat-sensitive currents in liposomes. Design the complementary test of whether it is the animal’s sole heat-withdrawal sensor, and explain what the liposome result leaves open.
cards.back: Delete TRPV1 and assay heat withdrawal; test combined loss of other candidate sensors if responses persist. Sufficiency in liposomes does not establish sole necessity in an animal. The stated rule allows several channels to contribute; combined TRPV1/TRPM3/TRPA1 loss abolished the tested response.
cards.quote: A channel may be sufficient for heat sensitivity in liposomes and still be one of several in the animal.
cards.section: The checklist for calling something the transducer

cards.front: After TMC1 rescues normal current in Tmc1/Tmc2-null hair cells, how could engineered cysteines support a pore-lining role, and which controls matter?
cards.back: Apply a cysteine-modifying reagent during recording. A rapid, irreversible permeation change in a variant with normal baseline current supports a pore role. Compare wild-type TMC1 and an unresponsive cysteine variant. The rule is that speed and residue specificity strengthen the case against an indirect effect; sufficiency remains untested.
cards.quote: so the speed and residue specificity of the change carry the argument; a slow change would suggest an indirect effect.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A candidate sensory channel produces no stimulus-evoked current in an otherwise insensitive cell, and the protein fails to reach the membrane. Does this exclude it as the transducer, and why?
cards.back: No. Sufficiency was not meaningfully tested at the membrane. Failed trafficking or a missing partner can explain a negative result; test sensitivity once membrane delivery and required partners are supported.
cards.quote: expression in a heterologous cell once the protein reaches the membrane.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Purified complexes of mosquito tuning odorant receptors with wasp Orco contained one tuning subunit and three Orco subunits. Can this establish the arrangement of every native insect odorant receptor?
cards.back: No. It establishes the observed arrangement in those purified, heterologous complexes; it does not establish a universal native stoichiometry.
cards.quote: Being purified, heterologous complexes, they do not show that every native insect receptor has a 1:3 arrangement.
cards.section: Insect odorant receptor structures, 2018 and 2024

cards.front: For free three-dimensional diffusion, rms spread is √(6Dt). With illustrative D ≈ 300 μm²/s and t = 40 μs, calculate the spread. Does it give a channel-binding time?
cards.back: t = 0.000040 s; √(6 × 300 × 0.000040) = 0.268 μm, about 270 nm. This is rms spread, not channel-binding time; finding and binding a channel also depend on geometry and binding kinetics.
cards.quote: The time to find and bind a channel also depends on geometry and binding kinetics.
cards.section: Diffusion against turnover in 40 microseconds

cards.front: One already-active enzyme produces messenger at 4000 molecules/s. For a 40 μs interval, calculate the expected count and the probability of at least one molecule, assuming Poisson production.
cards.back: Expected count λ = 4000 × 0.000040 = 0.16 molecule. P(at least one) = 1 − exp(−0.16) = 0.1479, about 15%. The fractional count is an expectation, not part of one molecule.
cards.quote: Molecules come whole, so 0.16 is an expected value:
cards.section: Diffusion against turnover in 40 microseconds

cards.front: In an illustrative rod cascade, hold total gain at 2000 cGMP per photon. If g is effective complexes per receptor and h is cGMP per complex, when do the steps contribute equally, and which dominates if g = 56?
cards.back: Using the stated fixed-product rule gh = 2000, equal gains require g = h = √2000 ≈ 44.7. At g = 56, h = 2000/56 ≈ 35.7, so the first step is larger. This comparison requires the same active-unit definition and fixed total; it is not a measured crossover.
cards.quote: they multiply equally at a first-step gain of about 45 (the square root of 2000);
cards.section: Rod and olfactory recording details

cards.front: Why are the Q10 of 23.5 and activation time constant of about 3.5 ms for purified rat TRPV1 different from molecular gain?
cards.back: Q10 describes temperature dependence; the time constant describes activation speed. They came from slow heating and a rapid heat jump, respectively. Neither is molecular gain.
cards.quote: A Q10 describes how steeply the response rises with temperature. It is not a molecular gain.
cards.section: TRPV1: two protocols, two numbers

cards.front: How do rods and cones signal light without firing action potentials?
cards.back: They hyperpolarize and regulate transmitter release with graded voltage changes. They are sensory neurons even though they do not spike.
cards.quote: their graded voltage regulates graded transmitter release rather than triggering action potentials
cards.section: Photoreceptors: primary or secondary?

cards.front: In mouse skin, deleting Piezo2 throughout the epidermis left substantial dynamic touch-afferent firing but reduced sustained firing. What model fits, and why can the fast firing not be assigned entirely to the afferent?
cards.back: A two-site model fits: the afferent detects touch and Merkel cells help sustain firing. But the manipulation affected all epidermal cells, so it did not isolate Merkel-cell contributions. The governing rule is that a cell-specific conclusion requires evidence that separates the contributing sites.
cards.quote: The results were most consistent with two receptor sites; the manipulation alone does not assign all the fast firing to the afferent.
cards.section: Merkel cells and Piezo2: two sites

cards.front: Pressure responses from reconstituted non-mammalian TMC orthologs and mechanically evoked currents from modified mammalian TMC preparations support sufficiency. What native hair-cell claim remains untested by these results?
cards.back: They do not test sufficiency of an unmodified native hair-cell complex. Preserve the distinction between orthologs, trafficking interventions or engineered tags, and the native complex.
cards.quote: None of these is an unmodified native hair-cell complex.
cards.section: TMC1 evidence in detail
